steps.prompt: Read this without a comma: “While the chef was cooking the soup boiled over.” Did you trip over it? Where did you expect the sentence to go after “cooking the soup”?

cards.title: A comma after an opener
cards.body: When something comes before the main sentence, a comma shows where the main sentence begins. Openers can be a word (However, Finally, Yes), a phrase (After lunch, For example, Running late) or a dependent clause (When the bell rang, Because it was cold).

cards.title: Openers and their commas
cards.text:
However, the plan didn’t work.
For example, the bake sale raised $200.
After the long game, we were starving.
When the bell rang, we ran outside.
cards.note: Clause at the end? Usually no comma: We ran outside when the bell rang.

cards.title: Commas around extra information
cards.telling: My sister who is twelve plays the drums.
cards.showing: My sister, who is twelve, plays the drums.
cards.note: If you can lift the words out and the sentence still works (My sister plays the drums), they are extra information: put a comma on both sides. Ms. Lee, our coach, smiled works the same way.

cards.title: Don’t lift out what you need
cards.body: “The students who finished early went outside.” Here “who finished early” tells you which students: lift it out and the meaning changes. Information you need takes no commas.

prompts: Pick one of your sentences. Read it with and without the comma. What changes for the reader?
How can you tell if a who or which clause needs commas?
